topic: My tomato plants have curling yellow leaves and I'm seeing tiny white insects underneath. What's going on and what should I do?

transcript.text: I’m seeing the same thing on my tomatoes—curling, yellowing leaves and tiny white insects underneath. I’ve got about 25 plants in a backyard row, mostly slicers with a few cherry types, and I’d prefer to avoid a harsh broad-spectrum spray if possible because I’m still harvesting. Are those most likely whiteflies, and would something like insecticidal soap be enough at this stage?

That “tiny white, winged critters” you’re seeing on the undersides of the leaves are almost always **whiteflies** (or a very close cousin, greenhouse whitefly). They feed on the leaf sap, cause the yellowing and curling you described, and can also serve as a vector for tomato viruses, so getting them under control quickly is key. ### Quick‑turn, low‑impact actions you can start today | Step | What to do | Why it works / tip | |------|------------|---------------------| | **1. Confirm the pest** | Look for the characteristic “moth‑shaped” white‑winged insects that rest in clusters on the leaf underside. If you shake a leaf and a cloud of tiny white flies flies out, you’ve got it. | Gives you confidence you’re targeting the right enemy. | | **2. Sticky traps** | Hang cheap yellow sticky cards (e.g., **Pegason™ Yellow Sticky Traps** or any garden‑center brand) about 12‑18 inches above the canopy. Replace every 2 weeks. | Traps adults, gives you a visual count of pressure, and reduces the breeding pool. | | **3. Insecticidal soap** | Use a ready‑made product such as **Safer Brand Insecticidal Soap** or **Bonide® Insecticidal Soap**. Dilute according to label (usually 5 mL ≈ 1 tsp per 1 L water). Spray **thoroughly on both sides** of every leaf, early morning or late evening, when temperatures are < 30 °C and no rain is forecast for 24 h. Repeat every 5–7 days until the population is gone (usually 3‑4 applications). | Soap breaks down the soft-bodied whitefly nymphs’ outer waxy layer. It’s OMRI‑approved and safe for the fruit you’re already picking. | | **4. Neem oil boost** | Mix **Neem‑Azal®** (or any 1‑2 % neem‑oil concentrate) at the label rate (≈ 1 tsp per 1 L water) and apply **after the soap spray has dried** (i.e., 24 h later). This gives a longer residual effect and also deters egg‑laying. | Neem’s azadirachtin interferes with whitefly development and deters adult females. | | **5. Physical removal** | For the most heavily infested branches, **prune out** the tops and drop them into a sealable bag for disposal. You can also **vacuum** the foliage with a handheld shop‑vac (set to low suction) to physically knock adults off. | Reduces the immediate load and prevents a few plants from acting as a source for the whole row. | | **6. Cultural tweaks** | • Keep the canopy open – thin out foliage to improve air flow and expose whiteflies to predators.
• Avoid any nitrogen‑heavy feeding during the outbreak; excess foliage encourages pest populations.
• Water at the base, not overhead, to keep the leaf‑undersides dry (soap works best on dry foliage). | A less humid, well‑ventilated canopy makes the environment less hospitable for whiteflies and for the secondary problems they cause (sooty mold, virus spread). | | **7. Encourage natural enemies** | If you have space, plant **marigold, alyssum, or sweet alyssum** a few feet away. These attract **lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps** that prey on whitefly nymphs. | Biological control can keep the population down after you’ve knocked it back with spray. | ### How you’ll know it’s working * **Sticky traps**: a sharp drop in the number of flies per trap after each spray. * **Leaf inspection**: fewer nymphs (tiny, pale‑green “crawlers”) on the undersides – you should see almost none after the 2nd‑3rd spray. * **Plant health**: yellowing and curling should stabilize, and new growth should look green and firm. ### Things to watch out for * **Spider mites** can look similar but they leave fine webbing and are more active in hot, dry weather. If you see little moving dots that spin silk, you may need a mite‑specific control (e.g., horticultural oil). * **Virus symptoms** (e.g., Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus) often appear as curling and yellowing even after the insects are gone. If the leaves keep deteriorating despite pest control, consider testing with your local extension office. * **Rain** within 24 h of a soap or neem application will wash it off, so plan around the forecast. --- #### Quick checklist for today 1. Set up 2–3 yellow sticky traps. 2. Mix and apply insecticidal soap on all foliage (pay special attention to undersides). 3. Re‑apply in 5‑7 days, adding a neem‑oil spray after the soap has dried. 4. Prune any heavily infested stems and discard them in a sealed bag. --- **Do you have any other pesticide residues already on the plants, or have you used any broad‑spectrum sprays this season?** Knowing that will help fine‑tune the timing and choice of the next spray.

transcript.text:
Yeah, the shake test nailed it — little cloud of white flies, classic whitefly. I've got maybe three or four of the twenty-five that are pretty rough, lower leaves pretty much gone and the curling is creeping up. The other two or so dozen are starting but not bad yet.

Here's where I'm stuck a little: I'm still pulling slicers off about ten of those plants every couple days, and I've got a heat wave coming this weekend, maybe 95 or so. If I do the soap spray, do I need to worry about it affecting fruit I'm picking that same day or the next, or is it fine as long as I'm not eating the leaves? And honestly, for those three or four that are really shot — is there any point hanging on, or should I just yank them, put them in the bag, and not risk the whole row?

**Short answer:** - **Insecticidal soap is safe on fruit you’re picking the same day** – just be sure the spray is completely dry before you harvest. - **Heat > 90 °F can increase the risk of leaf burn**, so apply the soap early in the morning (or late‑evening) and avoid direct midday sun. - **Remove the 3‑4 plants that are already “dead‑up”** – they act as a reservoir for whiteflies and can keep reinfesting the healthier vines. --- ### 1. Soap & fruit safety * **Residue:** Commercial insecticidal soaps (e.g., Safer Brand, Bonide, Bon‑pest) are just potassium salts of fatty acids. They break down in a few hours and are on the U.S. EPA’s **minimum‑risk** list. * **Harvest rule:** Spray, **wait until the coating is dry** (usually 30 min‑1 h in warm weather) and then pick. Rinse the fruit with a gentle water spray if you want extra peace of mind, but no waiting period is mandated. * **Do‑not** wash the fruit with detergent or a soap solution afterward – plain water or a quick rinse is fine. ### 2. Heat‑wave timing | Situation | What to do | |-----------|------------| | **Morning (6‑9 am) or evening (after sunset)** | Dilute soap at label rate, **coat both leaf surfaces** thoroughly. The cooler air lets the surfactant stay on the leaf long enough to rupture the whitefly nymphs. | | **Mid‑day > 90 °F** | Skip spraying. The hot, dry leaf can scorch, especially on tender new growth, and the soap can evaporate before it penetrates the insect. | | **After a rain forecast** | Postpone for at least 24 h; rain washes the soap off and you lose efficacy. | | **During the heat wave** | If you must spray, **water the base of the plant first** (so the soil is cool) and then apply the soap in a fine mist. Keep the foliage shaded for at least an hour (e.g., use a temporary shade cloth or garden umbrella). | ### 3. Should you keep the “dead‑up” plants? * **Why pull them:** * They provide a **breeding site** for whitefly adults and larvae. * Their wilted foliage is a perfect hiding place for flies that can *fly* onto healthier plants. * Removing them lowers the overall whitefly population pressure and reduces the chance of virus spread. * **How to remove:** 1. Cut the plant at the soil line with clean pruning shears. 2. **Bag the entire cut‑off plant** (plastic or newspaper) and seal it. 3. Dispose of the bag in the trash (or compost only if you’re sure it’s not disease‑laden). * **After removal:** Replace the space with a **row cover** (light‑weight garden fabric) for 7‑10 days while you finish the soap/Neem regime. That stops any surviving adults from colonizing the gap. ### 4. A quick “today’s action plan” | Time | Action | |------|--------| | **Tonight (if you can work in low light)** | Set out 2–3 **yellow sticky traps** about 12‑18 in. above the canopy. | | **Morning (6‑8 am, before the heat spikes)** | 1. Mix **insecticidal soap** at label strength (≈ 5 mL per liter of water).
2. Spray all foliage **until runoff**, covering the undersides.
3. Let it dry (≈ 30 min). | | **Mid‑day** | No spray. Keep plants well‑watered at the base (avoid overhead watering). | | **Late evening (after sunset)** | If you notice still‑active adults, give the plants a **quick blast of water** on the foliage to knock them off (they’ll fall onto the sticky traps). | | **Day 2–3** | Inspect sticky traps: if you’re still catching > 10 flies per trap, repeat the soap spray **again in 5 days**. | | **Day 5** | Add a **neem‑oil spray** (1 tsp per liter) **after the soap has dried**. This gives residual control for another 7‑10 days. | | **Whenever you see a plant with > 50 % of the lower canopy gone** | Pull it, bag it, and dispose of it. | ### 5. Bottom line for the heat wave - **Apply soap early, let it dry, then harvest** – no residue problem. - **Skip any midday applications**; the heat alone can damage leaves and reduce spray efficacy. - **Prune out the dead plants** now; it’s the fastest way to cut the whitefly “source” and protect the rest of the row. --- **One quick check:** Do you have any **broad‑spectrum insecticide residues** on the tomatoes already (e.g., pyrethroids, organophosphates)? If so, we’ll need to adjust the timing to avoid phytotoxicity and to stay within any pre‑harvest intervals. Let me know, and I can fine‑tune the spray schedule for you.

Alright, that tracks. I'll pull the three worst ones this morning and bag them up — honestly, at this point they're more liability than produce.

Quick answer to your question: no broad-spectrum sprays on the tomatoes this year. I did put copper fungicide on the peppers back in June, but nothing on the tomatoes, so I think I'm clear there.

Here's what's tripping me up though: you suggested row cover over the gaps where I'm pulling those three plants. My tomatoes are already about four feet tall and sprawling pretty aggressively, so I'm not really sure how I'd drape anything over a section without smothering or tangling the neighbors. Do you have a more practical way to keep the flies from re-colonizing those bare spots, or am I overthinking it and the sticky traps plus the soap rounds will handle it?

And one last timing thing — if I spray the soap Thursday morning and it dries by say 9 or 10, am I good to pick my usual harvest batch on Friday morning, or do you want me to push that to the afternoon?

**1. Keeping the freshly‑cleared gaps “fly‑free” without a full‑row cover** Because your plants are already 4 ft tall and spreading, a traditional row‑cover (light‑weight garden fabric) would be cumbersome. Here are three low‑effort alternatives that work just as well for a short‑term “buffer zone”: | Method | How to set it up | Why it works | Quick‑step checklist | |--------|-----------------|--------------|----------------------| | **a. DIY “mini‑fly‑screen” strips** | • Cut **UV‑stable, fine‑mesh insect netting** (e.g., ½‑inch mesh deli net or commercial butterfly net) into 3‑ft‑wide panels.
• Staple or zip‑tie the top edge of each panel to a **short (2‑ft) garden stake** driven into the soil a few inches in front of the gap.
• Use **clips or garden‑C‑ties** to attach the bottom edge of the net to the base of the tomato stems (or to a low stake) so the net hangs **just above the soil** and leaves the canopy untouched. | The mesh blocks adult whiteflies from flying straight into the empty space, but the canopy stays open for air flow and sunlight. | 1. Grab a roll of ½‑in mesh (≈ 3 yd is cheap). 2. Drive 4–5 stakes in a line where you removed the plants. 3. Hang the net, tension it lightly, and clip the bottom. | | **b. “Floating” cardboard/egg‑carton trap** | • Place a **large corrugated cardboard sheet** (or a few **egg‑cardboard trays**) flat on the soil where the plants were removed.
• Spray the top of the cardboard with a **1 % neem‑oil solution** (same dilution you’ll use for the plants).
• The oily surface deters whiteflies from landing, and the dark cardboard provides a visual “dead‑end” they won’t fly over. | Whiteflies prefer to land on green foliage or on a surface they can crawl onto. An oil‑treated, non‑host surface is unattractive, and the cardboard also blocks a few adult flies from hopping across the bare soil. | 1. Cut cardboard to fit the cleared spot (≈ 2 × 3 ft). 2. Spray with neem oil and let dry. 3. Replace every 5–7 days (or when it gets wet). | | **c. “Border‑spray” barrier** | • After you finish the soap + neem spray on the whole row, **apply a thin band of pure neem‑oil concentrate (no soap)** just along the edges of the cleared spot.
• Use a small brush or a pump‑sprayer set to “spot‑spray.” | Neem oil alone is a repellent for adult whiteflies; a concentrated band creates a “no‑go” line they’re reluctant to cross. It’s cheap and takes only a minute. | 1. Dilute neem oil to the label’s **full‑strength** (≈ 2 % active). 2. Paint a 6‑inch wide band on the soil and the lower stems bordering the gap. 3. Re‑apply after rain. | **Which one to pick?** - **If you have a roll of fine mesh** (often sold for “insect netting” in garden centers), the **mini‑fly‑screen** is the most reliable and lasts the whole heat‑wave. - If you’re short on time or netting, the **cardboard + neem** combo can be set up in 5 min and still gives a decent barrier. - The **neem‑oil border** is the fastest “one‑spray” fix; use it in addition to sticky traps and you’ll likely see a drop in new adult landings on the bare spots. **Bottom line:** You don’t need a full‑row cover. A modest barrier (mesh, oily cardboard, or neem strip) that sits **just above the soil** is enough to keep most adults from re‑infesting the gap while letting your tall vines breathe. --- **2. Harvest timing after an insecticidal‑soap spray** The EPA’s “minimum‑risk” status for potassium‑salt soaps means there is **no mandatory pre‑harvest interval**—the active ingredient degrades within minutes to a few hours. The only practical concern is **leaf burn or residue on the fruit** if the foliage is still wet when you pick. | Situation | Recommended harvest window | |-----------|----------------------------| | **Soap applied 6‑8 am, dry by 9‑10 am** | **Pick any fruit after the foliage is dry** – Friday morning is fine as long as the leaves are no longer tacky. A quick rinse under running water (or a gentle spray) will remove any trace. | | **Very hot, dry weather** ( > 95 °F, low humidity) | Soap dries faster, so **even a 30‑min interval** is enough. Harvest in the late‑morning or early afternoon. | | **If you spray later in the day (e.g., 2 pm)** | Wait until the **next morning** because the foliage may stay damp into the evening. | **Practical tip:** After you finish the Thursday spray, **run a quick hand‑test** on a leaf. If it feels dry and non‑sticky, go ahead and harvest the batch you plan for Friday. If it’s still a little damp, give it an extra 30 minutes or simply rinse the fruit before storage. --- ### Quick “to‑do” list for Thursday‑Friday 1. **Morning (≈ 6 am)** – Pull the three worst plants, bag them, and set your chosen barrier (mesh strip, cardboard‑neem, or neem band) over the empty space. 2. **6:15 am** – Mix and **apply insecticidal soap** to the whole row (both sides of every leaf). 3. **6:45 am** – Let it dry (sunny, 95 °F will dry it quickly). 4. **7 am** – **Inspect leaf surface**; if dry, you’re good to pick the usual harvest batch later that morning or at lunch. 5. **7:30 am** – Set **yellow sticky traps** if you haven’t already (one in the middle of the row, one near the newly cleared gap). 6. **Friday (anytime after 9 am)** – Harvest. Give fruit a quick rinse if you like extra peace of mind. 7. **Friday evening** – **Apply neem‑oil spray** (full‑strength 1‑2 % solution) as a follow‑up residual. This will protect you through the heat wave and into next week. --- **Final checklist** - [ ] Pull & bag dead plants. - [ ] Install barrier (mesh/cardia/easy neem band). - [ ] Soap spray early, let dry fully. - [ ] Harvest after foliage is dry (30 min + dry feel). - [ ] Set sticky traps. - [ ] Neem‑oil spray Friday evening. If you follow those steps, you’ll keep the whitefly pressure low, protect your fruit, and avoid the hassle of a full‑row cover. Let me know which barrier you choose or if you run into any surprise (e.g., a sudden rain after the Thursday spray) and we can tweak the plan on the fly. Happy picking!

Honestly, the cardboard is the only option I can pull off — I've got a stack of flattened boxes from my farm stand deliveries, so I can do that first thing this morning. The mesh is out unless I take a trip into town, and I'd rather not spend the morning at the store in this heat.

My one worry: in 95-degree weather, do you really want the cardboard laying right down on the bare soil, or should I prop it up a couple of inches so the ground can breathe? I don't want to bake the roots of the neighbors or turn that spot into a mold factory.

And one last thing on your schedule — if I put on the neem Friday evening as you suggested, I've got my next picking batch coming Saturday morning. Is that fine, or should I push that harvest to Sunday to be safe?

### 1.  Cardboard barrier – how to set it up so the soil “breathes”

**What you’ll do**

1. **Lay the cardboard on a shallow frame** so it’s 2–3 inches off the ground, not flat on the soil.  
2. **Simple frame idea:**  
   * Use a few **2‑ft lengths of ¼‑in PVC pipe** (or a couple of garden‑stake pieces) and push them into the soil in a rectangle around the empty spot (one pipe at each corner).  
   * Slip a **cheese‑cloth or old garden fabric** over the top of the pipes, then lay the flattened boxes on top of that fabric. The fabric lets water pass through while keeping the cardboard from sagging into the soil.  
3. **Secure the edges** with a garden‑twine or a small **U‑shaped garden staple** so wind doesn’t lift the cardboard.  

**Why the “raised” set‑up matters**

| Issue | What happens if cardboard sits flat | Why a 2‑3‑in lift helps |
|-------|--------------------------------------|------------------------|
| **Soil aeration** | Soil under the cardboard can become compacted, limiting oxygen to the root zone of the neighboring plants. | The fabric + pipe gap lets air circulate and moisture drain. |
| **Moisture‑related mold** | A wet cardboard pad becomes a perfect breeding ground for fungi and bacteria, especially in 95 °F humidity. | Water can drip through the fabric, drying the cardboard faster and preventing standing‑water pockets. |
| **Root heat** | Direct contact with a sun‑heated cardboard sheet can act like a “black blanket” and raise soil temperature a few degrees. | The air space buffers the heat, keeping the root zone cooler. |

**Quick “set‑up” steps (5 min)**  

1. **Gather**: 4–5 short PVC pieces (or sturdy wooden stakes), garden‑twine, a piece of old garden fabric or cheese cloth, your flattened boxes.  
2. **Insert** the stakes into the ground at the corners of the cleared spot (about 6 in deep).  
3. **Lay** the fabric across the top of the stakes, pulling it taut.  
4. **Place** the cardboard on top, overlapping the edges a little so there are no gaps.  
5. **Tie** the fabric’s corners to the stakes with twine to keep everything steady.  

You can leave the barrier in place for the whole heat wave (7–10 days). When the whitefly pressure eases, just pull everything out, compost the cardboard, and re‑level the soil.

---

### 2.  Neem‑oil spray → harvest timing

**Neem oil is a “minimum‑risk” pesticide** (the active azadirachtin is a natural plant compound). Most extension services list a **pre‑harvest interval (PHI) of 0 days** for fruits, meaning you can pick the same day once the spray has dried. However, there are two practical points to keep in mind:

| Concern | How it shows up | What to do |
|---------|----------------|------------|
| **Residue on the fruit surface** | A thin oily film can make the fruit feel slightly slick if you pick it while the spray is still wet. | Wait **until the foliage is completely dry** (usually 30 – 60 min in 95 °F weather). |
| **Potential flavor impact** | Some growers notice a faint “green‑pepper” note if they harvest **immediately** after a heavy neem application and the fruit is still soft. | If you’re picking **ripe, firm tomatoes**, a short 30‑min dry period is fine; if you’re picking very soft, early‑fruit, give it **2–3 hours** or wait until the next morning. |

**Your schedule**

- **Thursday morning:** soap spray (dry by ~9‑10 am).  
- **Friday morning:** harvest the batch you normally pick – **yes, you’re good**; just be sure the leaves are dry before you start plucking.  
- **Friday evening:** apply neem‑oil spray (full‑strength 1‑2 % per label). The spray will dry quickly in the heat (≈ 30 min).  
- **Saturday morning harvest:** also fine **as long as the foliage is dry** when you pick. The oil film is well‑below the PHI limit, and a short drying period is all that’s needed.  
- **If you want extra peace of mind** (e.g., you’re worried about a lingering scent or you have ultra‑sensitive customers), **push the Saturday batch to Sunday** – but it’s not required.

**Bottom line:** **Saturday morning pick is safe**; just give the neem‑oil about 30‑45 minutes to dry, then harvest. If you notice a slight slickness on a fruit, a quick rinse under cool water (no soap) will remove any trace.

---

### 3.  Quick “to‑do” recap for the next 48 hours

| Day / Time | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| **Thursday – early** | Pull & bag the 3 dead plants. |
| **Thursday – 6 am** | Build the raised cardboard barrier (PVC‑stake + fabric + boxes). |
| **Thursday – 6:15 am** | Mix & spray **insecticidal soap** (full label rate) on all foliage. |
| **Thursday – 6:45 am** | Check leaf dryness; if dry, go ahead with any planned harvest that day. |
| **Thursday – 7 am** | Set **yellow sticky traps** (one in the middle of the row, one at the edge of the cardboard zone). |
| **Friday – early** | Harvest the usual batch (leaves dry → ok). |
| **Friday – evening (after sun down)** | Apply **neem‑oil spray** (full‑strength 1‑2 % solution) over the entire row, including the cardboard barrier. |
| **Saturday – early** | Wait 30‑45 min for the neem to dry, then harvest the next batch. |
| **Saturday – after harvest** | If rain is forecast, re‑apply a **light neem‑oil band** only on the cardboard edges (no need for a full spray). |
| **Sunday (optional)** | Inspect sticky traps; if you still see > 10 flies per trap, repeat a **soap + neem** round on Monday morning. |

---

**Final tip:** After you finish the heat‑wave cycle, give the soil in the cleared spot a good **organic amendment** (compost or well‑rotted manure). That will help the roots of the neighboring tomatoes recover any temporary compaction caused by the cardboard barrier.

Good luck, and enjoy that fresh‑tomato taste—whiteflies will be a thing of the past soon enough! If you run into any new symptoms (e.g., soggy leaves, sudden leaf drop) just let me know. Happy harvesting!
